bio-oxygen-dissociation.title: The oxygen dissociation curve and the Bohr shift
bio-oxygen-dissociation.caption: In the lungs haemoglobin is almost fully saturated. In respiring tissue, where pO₂ is low, the steep middle of the curve means a small fall in pO₂ releases a lot of oxygen. More CO₂ shifts the curve right (lower affinity), so even more is released; fetal haemoglobin's curve lies to the left (higher affinity).
bio-oxygen-dissociation.alt: S-shaped oxygen dissociation curves of percentage saturation against partial pressure of oxygen, with the curve for high carbon dioxide shifted right and fetal haemoglobin shifted left.
description: The horizontal axis is the partial pressure of oxygen in kilopascals, from 0 to 14. The vertical axis is percentage saturation of haemoglobin, from 0 to 100.
The adult curve is S-shaped (sigmoid): flat at low partial pressure, steep in the middle, and levelling off near 97% at the partial pressure in the lungs (about 13 kPa).

The curve at high carbon dioxide (the Bohr effect) lies to the right of it: at the same partial pressure, haemoglobin is less saturated, so it has given up more oxygen. An arrow at 4 kPa shows the extra oxygen unloaded.
The fetal haemoglobin curve lies to the left: at the same partial pressure it is more saturated, so it can take oxygen from the mother's blood.

Shaded bands mark the partial pressures typical of respiring tissue and of the lungs. Curves are drawn from the Hill equation (n = 2.7) with P50 about 3.6 kPa for adult haemoglobin, 4.4 kPa at high CO₂ and 2.5 kPa for fetal haemoglobin: illustrative values, and real ones vary.

review.notes: Round 1: Bohr shift exaggerated (P50 4.8); now 4.4 kPa and labelled illustrative. Round 2: approve.

chem-br2-bromonium.title: Adding Br₂ to cyclohexene: anti addition through a bromonium ion

law-duty-of-care.title: Does a duty of care exist?
law-duty-of-care.caption: After Robinson, start with precedent rather than a three-stage test. Precedent can deny a duty as well as recognise one. Only a genuinely novel situation calls for incremental reasoning by analogy, with the Caparo factors weighed together. Separately, there is generally no duty to protect others from harm caused by third parties or to rescue, unless an exception applies.
law-duty-of-care.alt: Decision tree for whether a duty of care exists in negligence, following Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire Police, Caparo v Dickman and the omissions rule.
description: Question 1: is the claim that the defendant's own act made the claimant worse off, or, if it is about failing to protect them from harm, does an exception apply (the defendant created the danger, assumed responsibility, or had control of the third party or the source of danger)? If no, there is generally no duty: no general duty to prevent harm caused by third parties or to rescue (Smith v Littlewoods; N v Poole BC).

Question 2: is the situation genuinely novel, with no precedent deciding it? If no, follow the precedent: there is a duty where it recognises one (for example road users, doctor and patient), provided the kind of harm to this claimant was reasonably foreseeable; there is no duty where precedent excludes one (Robinson).

If the situation is novel: develop the law incrementally, by analogy with established categories, weighing reasonable foreseeability of damage, proximity, and whether it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty, together rather than as separate gates (Caparo; Robinson).

review.notes: Round 1: REJECTED (not novel ≠ duty exists; omissions branch a dead end; Caparo as sequential gates). Rebuilt to follow Robinson. Round 2: approve; the lesson's own K: line, which contradicted Robinson, was corrected.

phys-fbd-slope.title: Box pushed up a rough slope by a horizontal force
phys-fbd-slope.caption: Four forces, each with a physical source. Weight acts from the centre of mass straight down; the normal force is perpendicular to the slope; friction acts down the slope, opposing the motion; the push P is horizontal. Because P presses the box into the slope, N is bigger than mg here: resolving perpendicular to the slope gives N = mg cos θ + P sin θ.
phys-fbd-slope.alt: Free-body diagram of a box on a slope at angle theta, with weight down, normal force perpendicular to the slope, friction down the slope and a horizontal push.
description: A right-angled slope rising to the right at angle theta, with a box resting on it.

Friction, f, is drawn along the contact face, pointing down the slope. The push, P, is a horizontal arrow arriving at the box from the left.

Because P is horizontal, part of it presses the box into the slope, so the normal force is bigger than mg cos theta: N = mg cos theta + P sin theta. With m = 2 kg, P = 15 N and theta = 25 degrees, N is about 24 N against a weight of about 20 N, and the arrows are drawn to that scale (friction's size is illustrative).

chem-reaction-classes.title: Classifying an organic reaction
chem-reaction-classes.caption: Ask what happens to the starting molecule. Two molecules joining into one is addition; a group swapped for another is substitution; a small molecule lost to form a double bond is elimination. Oxidation, reduction, condensation and hydrolysis are named by what is gained or lost.
chem-reaction-classes.alt: A decision tree: does the number of molecules fall? If yes, addition. If no, is one group replaced by another? If yes, substitution; if no, is a small molecule removed to leave a multiple bond? If yes, elimination; otherwise a rearrangement.
description: First question: do two reactant molecules become one product? Yes means addition, as in ethene + HBr.
Otherwise: is one atom or group replaced by another? Yes means substitution, as in bromoethane + OH⁻.
Otherwise: is a small molecule such as H₂O or HBr removed, leaving a double bond? Yes means elimination; if not, the atoms have rearranged.
